#724. In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor—encapsulated within a GalNAc–lipid nanoparticle—leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

#723. Elon Musk Is Portrayed on ‘SNL’: “The Worst Thing South Africa Has Ever Done”

Jeremy Culhane plays the character in the show’s latest attempt to assess its relationship with the mogul.

Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars to get humiliated at the polls, but at least he came away with an SNL parody.Jeremy Culhane played the mogul in an appearance with Weekend Update’s Colin Jost as he tried to make sense of his bruising electoral losses. The actor offered a persuasive impression of the mogul’s halting speeches and nonsensical attempts to change the subject with talk of a future that won’t happen. “Imagine,” Culhane’s Musk ended a sentence several times non-sequiturishly.A few days after his major campaign investments came up fruitless (and in a week when his Cybertruck was officially deemed a failure, compounding the injury), comic Musk sought to change the subject“You’re in the news because you wasted half a billion dollars on the midterms… almost all the candidates you backed lost,” Jost said. Related Stories TV Druski Embodies Elizabeth Holmes in 'You Can See Everything' Spoof on 'SNL' TV James Talarico Crashes 'SNL' Cold Open, Apologizes for Texting Us So Much

“I’m in the news because my car did a flip… it was like a freaking Hot Wheel,” Musk replied with a Buttheadian enthusiasm.Jost pointed out the irony that “you moved to Texas because California was run by Democrats” and now Texas would be too. “How does that make you feel?” Jost asked.“Bad,” Musk said, before cluelessly changing the topic back to a car flip and barrage of so-you-know-uhs the mogul is known for. (In real life, Musk tried to turn the losses into vindication for the conspiracy theories that he was involved in rigging the 2024 election.)The show’s writers piled on when they had Musk ask Grok to treat him to an “epic vulgar-roast” (Culhane’s coinage for what Musk considers a major burn) and the AI chatbot came back with, “You’re the worst thing South Africa has ever done;” “When you’re on TV it feels like a episode of ‘Hate on the Spectrum’;” and “If you have 100 more kids, maybe one of them will talk to you.”Musk has been in the pop-cultural spotlight this fall with Alex Gibney’s four-hour investigative documentary, which deconstructs the myth of mogul and makes a case he is far more dangerous than caricaturist appearances in Hollywood productions may suggest. Musk has recently has been buying up spectrum, spending $1 billion on Skydance and taking flack for allegedly turning off Starshield and potentially endangering Ukrainian lives.The character had recently been played by Mike Myers, as in a cold open appearance a year ago as he maniacally bellowed “Legalize Comedy” behind portrayals of Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and other appearances in which he did an unhinged air-pounding two-first dance. That impression had a lot of scenery-chewing swings (and more than its share of Mike Myers being Mike Myers), while Culhane Saturday night was more effectively restrained and on-point, leaving the possibility he might be reprising the character on future SNL episodes.Gibney’s film notes how Musk has been savvy at doing cartoonish enough behaviors that people tend to underestimate him, a point that was underscored even in the sketch when, after he went off one more time about a vulgar epic-roast and a car flip, Jost said “I cannot believe you’re the richest person in the world.”

SNL has a tricky relationship with the mogul. Five years ago, Musk himself hosted in an appearance that prompted a boycott from multiple cast members, led to Chloe Fineman crying and is now seen as a bad choice to cuddle-ify a toxic figure.The appearance Saturday could be seen the show’s attempt to atone for that misstep, though some critics will say it further turns Musk into a colorful media character at the expense of his status as a graver threat.

Two spacewalking astronauts will finish upgrading the International Space Station's power system today (Nov. 5), and you can watch the action live.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and the Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk will install the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) today, during a roughly seven-hour spacewalk that's scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT).

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA, beginning at 7 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT).

Today's extravehicular activity (EVA) will be the second in a week for Menon and Kutryk, who installed the station's seventh iROSA during an Oct. 29 spacewalk. That excursion was the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the ISS to date, and the first EVA for a Canadian astronaut since 2019.

Today's spacewalk will wrap up an ambitious ISS power upgrade that has taken more than five years to pull off.

"The installation job will complete the years-long process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts," NASA officials wrote about the EVA in a blog post on Tuesday (Nov. 3). That's a boost of about 30%.

Menon and Kutryk are currently sharing the ISS with five other astronauts — NASA's Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov.

Delaney, Kutryk, Teteryatnikov and Watkins arrived at the ISS on Oct. 1, on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission. Dubrov, Kikina and Menon got there in mid-July, aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

Michael Jackson’s Thriller vaults 13-2 on the Billboard 200 (dated Nov. 14), scoring its highest rank on the list since the spring of 1984, when it logged its 37th and final week at No. 1 on the April 14-dated list. Thriller continues to hold the record for the most weeks atop the list for an album by a singular artist. (Only the film soundtrack to West Side Story spent more weeks at No. 1: 54, in 1962-63.)

The Billboard 200 chart ranks the most popular albums of the week in the U.S. based on multi-metric consumption as measured in equivalent album units, compiled by Luminate. Units comprise album sales, track equivalent albums (TEA) and streaming equivalent albums (SEA). Each unit equals one album sale, or 10 individual tracks sold from an album, or 2,500 ad-supported or 1,000 paid/subscription on-demand official audio and video streams generated by songs from an album. The new Nov. 14, 2026-dated chart will be posted in full on Billboard‘s website on Nov. 10. For all chart news, follow @billboard and @billboardcharts on both X and Instagram.

In the tracking week of Oct. 30 through Nov. 5 — thus, including Halloween — Thriller earned 55,000 equivalent album units (up 89%), boosted by seasonal spooky streams of the set’s title track, as well as new physical versions of the album that were released. Of that unit total, SEA units comprise 32,000 (up 37%, equaling 34.34 million on-demand official streams of the set’s songs; it moves 14-5 on Top Streaming Albums), album sales comprise 22,000 (up 335%; it rises 14-3 on Top Album Sales) and TEA units comprise 1,000 (up 30%).

On Oct. 30, Thriller was reissued across three new vinyl variants (two color editions and a liquid-filled version) and a cassette tape. The album’s 22,000 sales for the week mark its largest single-week sales sum in nearly four years, since it shifted 23,000 (Dec. 31, 2022-dated list).

Notably, of Thriller’s 22,000 sold in the latest tracking week, vinyl purchases account for 19,000 — the album’s largest sales week on vinyl since Luminate began electronically tracking sales in 1991.

With Thriller’s jump to No. 2, Jackson has his highest rank on the Billboard 200 in more than a decade, since the posthumous album Xscape debuted and peaked at No. 2 on the May 31, 2014-dated chart.

Notably, Thriller has appeared on the Billboard 200 each year since 2009, following Jackson’s death that June. It has resided in the top 20 each week since early May, with 15 consecutive weeks in the top 10 through August, spurred by the record-setting biopic Michael.

#720. Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków

The 34th edition of Camerimage kicked off with Luca Guadagnino’s 'Artificial' and included honors for Darren Aronofsky and the THR Visionary Award for cinematographer Janusz Kamiński.

The AI elephant in the room took center stage on Saturday at the opening night of the 34th Camerimage Film Festival.

Instead of avoiding the divisive issue of artificial intelligence, the Polish fest, the world’s leading festival for the celebration of the art of cinematography, doubled down.

For the opening address, in place of festival director Marek Żydowicz, Camerimage sent a humanoid robot, called “Edward Warchocki,” on stage. The slightly tottering, Polish-speaking android addressed the crowd before Żydowicz joined it for an extended back-and-forth about the role of AI in cinema. The “hopes and threats” of the technology, Żydowicz stressed, would be a major talking point throughout the seven-day event in Toruń. Related Stories Movies Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why "Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians" Movies PÖFF Stands With Ukraine: A Look at Films Featured at Tallinn Made Despite, and Because of, the War

The theme ran through the three-hour ceremony at the city’s Jordanki Culture Centre, which was regularly interspersed with video messages from Francis Ford Coppola, Gal Gadot, Christopher Nolan, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Steven Spielberg and Ben Affleck, each weighing in on AI in entertainment.

Few filmmakers are as closely associated with the debate as Darren Aronofsky, who was honored with Camerimage’s honorary Award for Director. A vocal advocate of generative AI in filmmaking since launching his AI studio Primordial Soup last year, the Requiem for a Dream and Black Swan helmer said it was his third visit to the festival and that he hoped to keep coming back.

“The reason I come back is because there are very rarely film festivals that celebrate the collaboration of everyone,” he said. “They’re very focused on not just the flashy names and that’s really incredible because it honors everyone who makes films possible for people like me.”

Other honorees included Karolina Gruszka, one of Poland’s most acclaimed film and stage actresses, who received the Marshal of the Kujawy Pomorze Region Film Award. Gruszka, who appeared in David Lynch’s last feature, Inland Empire (which was shot in Poland) paid tribute to the late director as a “master investigator” of stories.

Polish cinematographer Janusz Kamiński, longtime Spielberg collaborator and two-time Oscar winner (for Schindler’s List and Saving Private Ryan) received The Hollywood Reporter’s Visionary Award for contributions to cinematography. The festival also paid tribute to the late great Polish director Andrzej Wajda (Man of Iron, Ashes and Diamonds), a century after his birth and a decade after his death, with a performance by the Polish Radio Choir – Lusławice giving an a cappella reinterpretation of the music from Wajda’s most important films. Poland’s Senate has declared 2026 “The Year of Wajda.”

The night’s opening film — Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI origin story Artificial, starring Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever — continued the AI theme. Guadagnino and cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed took the stage to discuss the film and the issues it raises. When it comes to cinema, said Sayeed, AI was “just a tool, like any other.” Guadagnino, who shot Artificial on 35 mm and has shown no interest in using AI for his work, said the real issues raised by Artificial are about “what they call the tech oligarchs, the tech bros” and the unprecedented levels of power, “economic power and political power” they have acquired over our lives. Simon Rich’s script, he said, offered “an unprecedented setup for showing how very few people control societies.” Neon is releasing Artificial in the U.S. on Dec. 25.

The Camerimage festivities were overshadowed by events elsewhere in the country. The ceremony began with a minute’s silence for the victims of a mass shooting in Kraków earlier in the day. According to reports, at least six people were killed and more than a dozen injured when a gunman, suspected of far-right ties, drove into the city’s historic Main Market Square and opened fire. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three more bodies were later found at the suspect’s home, making it Poland’s deadliest shooting in decades. Local politicians scheduled to speak at the opening acknowledged the severity of the attack before the program began.

#719. Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss Attend Travis Kelce’s Chiefs Game in Kansas City

The longtime friends reunited to watch the Chiefs take on the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium on Nov. 8.

Taylor Swift had some familiar company as she cheered on husband Travis Kelce and the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday (Nov. 8).

The 36-year-old pop superstar watched the Chiefs take on the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, joined by longtime friend Karlie Kloss. The supermodel, 34, was also among the guests at Swift and Kelce’s July 3 wedding at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Swift and Kloss appeared in good spirits as they watched the Chiefs take the field for their ninth game of the season. The “Shake It Off” singer wore a red sweater as she cheered on Kelce alongside her parents, Andrea and Scott Swift. Sunday’s matchup also marked a career milestone for the tight end, who made his 200th NFL appearance.

Swift and Kloss first struck up a friendship in 2013, eventually becoming close enough to share the cover of Vogue in 2015. Their relationship later became the subject of speculation when they were seen together less frequently. In August 2023, Kloss attended Swift’s Eras Tour show in Los Angeles.

Sunday marked Swift’s fourth appearance at a Chiefs game this season. She previously attended the team’s Oct. 18 home game against the Los Angeles Chargers, watching from a suite alongside musician Este Haim and basketball star Caitlin Clark.

Earlier in the season, Swift attended the Chiefs’ Sept. 14 game against the Denver Broncos, where she was spotted with actor Tom Cruise. She returned to Arrowhead Stadium on Sept. 20 for the team’s matchup against the Indianapolis Colts.

Swift’s Oct. 18 appearance at Arrowhead Stadium came just one day after a surprise appearance at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles, where she delivered the live debut of “The Fate of Ophelia” during a short set. The event honored filmmaker John Carpenter, Colman Domingo and Charlize Theron.

#718. Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results

German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

Though it has been two days since Israel's parliamentary elections, German politicians are still being cautious to respond, as it is still unclear who will lead Israel's new government.

Although the right-wing bloc, including religious hardliners, led by incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, neither has a clear path to a governing majority in the Knesset.

Forming a coalition government is likely to be extremely difficult.

Martin Giese, spokesperson for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, declined to comment at Wednesday's regular government press conference in Berlin.

But he did stress that Germany has been in contact with numerous officials and politicians in Israel via Germany's ambassador. "The Jewish state and Germany are inextricably linked by our history, and we will do everything we can to work well with any future government," Wadephul said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One concern for the German government is providing aid to the people in Gaza, and protracted coalition negotiations could delay necessary progress.

"Winter is coming, and it will be difficult," Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan, currently visiting Lebanon, warned in an interview with Politico. She underlined that there must be more opportunities for aid organizations to provide crucial assistance in Gaza and that it cannot wait for coalition negotiations.

In interviews with DW and broadcaster RTL, she spoke about the recent increase in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.

"The radical settler violence must be stopped. The Netanyahu government remains in office on an interim basis, and this means that this situation must still be brought to an end," she said.

All settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories is considered illegal under international law.

Relations between Germany and Israel are traditionally close, in part because of Germany's historical responsibility for Nazi Germany's murder of millions of Jews during the Holocaust.

Recently, however, the German government has distanced itself from Netanyahu's policies, at least in its public rhetoric.

Most recently, Wadephul said after a major Israeli military operation near the city of Hebron: "Under international law, Israel is quite clearly obligated to uphold and protect the rights of Palestinians as well." Around 3,000 Palestinians were driven from their homes during the operation, which followed the reported killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinians.

In Berlin, there has long been speculation about whether Germany's policy toward Israel might change after Israel's 2026 election.

So far, one thing is clear: Unlike numerous other countries, including some in Europe, Germany does not intend to recognize a Palestinian state for the time being.

At the same time, Germany hopes that the future government will no longer include religious extremists, and in some cases far-right, politicians such as the current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"I think it would be best for Israel to form a government that is closer to the center of the political spectrum," Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in the Bundestag, told DW. "Of course, that's something the people, and above all the elected politicians, will have to figure out. But it's encouraging that so many people participated in the election."

The Arab-majority parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel made large gains in this election. They are usually classified as part of the current opposition camp. The historic results by these parties could lead them to play a kingmaker role in coalition formation.

However, Netanyahu’s bloc have ruled out working with the Arab-majority parties.

Eisenkot's opposition bloc has not yet said whether it would be willing to form such a coalition, but one of the Arab-majority parties, United Arab List/Ra'am, featured a Jewish candidate, and has stated its willingness to work with Eisenkot’s bloc to unseat Netanyahu.

Hardt believes a minority government led by Eisenkot and supported by parties representing Arab Israelis is conceivable.

"The major campaign carried out by Netanyahu's camp, aimed primarily against Arab Israelis, greatly mobilized the opposition, to the point where his camp no longer has a majority."

The vice president of the German Bundestag, Green Party politician Omid Nouripour, told DW: "Frankly, after all the turmoil that has occurred — for example, regarding judicial reform — this is good news for Israeli democracy."

This article was originally published in German.

#717. To Make a Doc About a Nomadic Cyclist, the ‘Perfect Road’ Filmmakers Spent 3 Months in a Campervan

Adam and Christian Bonke recall how they and their cinematographer followed Maximilian Schnell in a "not so big" vehicle with "a lot of equipment" to shoot material for the film now screening at Tallinn.

For their documentary Perfect Road, Danish directors and cousins Adam and Christian Bonke followed nomadic cyclist Maximilian Schnell on an extreme journey across some of Europe’s highest mountain passes. The film documents his journey, offers a character study and serves up a meditation on modern life and our priorities and life choices.

Elk Film and Dogwoof produced Perfect Road, with Andreas Dalsgaard, Anna Godas, Oli Harbottle, Miriam Nørgaard serving as producers. Jonatan Mose served as cinematographer, with editing handled by Martin Anthon. Related Stories Movies Janusz Kaminski, the Polish Cameraman Who Taught Hollywood How to See Movies Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków

Perfect Road, which world premiered at Zurich, is now screening at the 30th anniversary edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia. It shows how the road brings freedom and adventure, but also grueling physical and mental challenges. And that is not only true for Schnell but also the directors and their cinematographer.

“We ended up living in a campervan for three months,” recalls Adam Bonke. “It was three grown-up men in a not so big campervan with a lot of equipment. And then we had a small a smaller car, like a satellite, that we could send out on the tiny roads where the campervan couldn’t go.”

Adds Christian Bonke: “It was such a headache because you had to put water into the car, you had to empty the toilet. So when we were done shooting for the day, we had to take care of all that.”

The filmmakers considered various strategies for capturing footage. Initially, they wanted to use several different camera people over the course of the three-month adventure. “But then our DP was kicked out by his girlfriend,” Christian Bonke tells THR. “So he said, ‘I’m going to do all three months. This is perfect for me.’ And Adam and I took turns.”

It may not have been a holiday or super-comfortable, but Adam Bonke tells THR: “It was comfortable enough.” And it allowed the filmmakers to get a better feel for Schnell’s life choices. “He said, ‘I’m trading comfort for freedom,'” the co-director explains. “I think that’s that’s such a nice thing to say and really frames the film perfectly.”

The Danish filmmaker duo actually still fondly looks back at the experience shooting Perfect Road. “We often talk about how we miss those days. It was so beautiful,” says Christian Bonke. “You felt embraced by nature. And after meeting Max, we were completely hit by how conventional and boring [traditional life can be] and how many constraints our lives had at home. So we could get a little glimpse of living his way.”

#716. Janusz Kaminski, the Polish Cameraman Who Taught Hollywood How to See

The cinematographer behind 'Schindler's List,' 'Saving Private Ryan' and 'The Diving Bell and the Butterfly' is THR's Visionary of the Year.

Like pretty much every great cinematographer, Janusz Kamiński is Polish. As much as any single artist of his generation, he has also taught Hollywood how to see.

Kamiński, winner of THR‘s 2026 Visionary Award for excellence in cinematography, presented at the Camerimage festival on Saturday, grew up in Ziębice, a small town where, as he remembers it, the world was gray. “Although we didn’t feel it was bleak, it was bleak,” Kamiński says. “No billboards. No advertisements. The streets were dark. People dressed in darker tones.” In winter, the houses were heated with coal, and the smoke from every chimney stayed in the air. “The air had this thickness in it, like a fog, because of the coal particles.” Related Stories Movies To Make a Doc About a Nomadic Cyclist, the 'Perfect Road' Filmmakers Spent 3 Months in a Campervan Movies Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków

But there was a lot of longing in that gray. “Poland is a very lyrical country, to some degree,” he says. “There’s that melancholy, that certain wish for something else.” Theater troupes passed through, and the local cinema promised a world beyond the town. “We were exposed to work that we didn’t experience in real life, but we wanted to experience,” Kamiński says. “The primary reason I left home is because of the theater and movies, and a life of color.”

Kamiński left Poland as a political refugee in 1981, dreaming of American movies. He spoke no English. Landing in Chicago, he spent two years learning the language and then enrolled part-time at Columbia College. In an introductory filmmaking class, he found himself in a group of five. “We had to each pick: One would be the writer, one the actor, one the director, one the producer, and one the cinematographer,” he recalls. “We literally picked straws. I got cinematography. I was 22.”

It was love at first sight. “I found out I really enjoyed creating images. It was just fascinating for me to see the flickering image on 16 mm black and white,” he says. “Just that mystery: Will it be in focus? Will it be properly exposed? Will it have a story?” A professor told him he was good at it and should keep going. “This is not a sad story, but it was the first time anyone every told me I was good at something,” says Kamiński. “In Poland, when I grew up, nobody’s parents said that kind of thing. It was: You have food, you eat, you’re good.”

All his classmates at Columbia wanted to direct, so Kamiński shot their movies. He loaded a station wagon with equipment every weekend and made student films, and picked up commercial work as a camera assistant, an electrician and a grip. One commercial spot a month would pay $250. “My rent was $280, so I was doing good,” he says. “I had a job, and for an immigrant, it’s essential that we support ourselves, because there was no mommy, no daddy, no cousins.”

In the early days, The Hollywood Reporter came to his aid. Back then, in the back of the magazine, THR ran lists of movies going into production, including location shoots. “That’s how I got my first jobs, through The Hollywood Reporter,” says Kamiński. “I’d look at that films listed and I wouldn’t call on a Tom Cruise movie, but if it was something like Bambis from Hell, I’d call the producer up and say ‘Hi, my name is Janusz Kamiński. I’m a cinematographer. Would you like to look at my work? I got my first two features from that.”

Kaminski knew Chicago would not get him to Hollywood. “Most of the movies that would originate in California would come into Chicago and use secondary crew members,” he says. “I don’t want to be secondary.” His girlfriend filled out an application to the American Film Institute, and he was accepted. “That was 1986/87. I moved to California, another place I’d never been to. I had no car.” He rented a place within walking distance of campus.

A classmate’s husband, a cinematographer, was shooting a movie for Roger Corman and needed a key grip. Kamiński took the job. “Meanwhile, the gaffer quit. So I said, I like lighting. Let me. So I became the gaffer.” He kept shooting second unit and small independent films while he finished school.

The real break came through his demo reel. A friend of a friend was Diane Keaton’s assistant. “He shows my demo reel, my student film demo reel, to Diane Keaton and, suddenly, I have a job shooting for Diane Keaton.” The film was Wildflower, a period TV movie with Patricia Arquette and Beau Bridges. Steven Spielberg saw it and offered Kaminski another TV gig, Class of ‘61, a pilot Spielberg was producing. The show, about West Point cadets on the eve of the Civil War, didn’t get picked up. But Spielberg liked what he saw. When the pilot wrapped, the two men met. “He says, ‘I’d like you to film my next movie. I’m doing a black and white movie called Schindler’s List. Would you be interested?’”

Spielberg first went off to do Jurassic Park. “It took him eight to nine months to finish editing,” Kamiński recalls. “All that time I knew I had a job coming with Steven Spielberg. But nobody believed me. Only when I shot the movie, it became reality.”

With Spielberg, Kamiński went home to Poland. The film he shot there, full of the gray light and smoky streets he had grown up in, changed how Hollywood shot history. He says the two of them barely discussed the visual style beforehand. “We knew it would be shot in Poland and be black-and-white, but we didn’t have a deep, in-depth conversation about how we’re going to make this movie,” he recalls. “We just wanted to strip away anything that would take us away from the story, so there was no crane, no dolly and no Steadicam. I brought in the idea of using handheld.”

Schindler’s List won Kamiński his first Oscar for Best Cinematography. Saving Private Ryan won him a second. The script for that film, he points out, contained one sentence about the landing at Normandy: “Now the troops land at Normandy. That’s it. So as a cinematographer, you have to create the language that corresponds to the story, to the emotions, to the sets and the locations.” What he and Spielberg came up with, all handheld, drained of color and chaotic, rewrote the language of the war movie.

Shooting Julian Schnabel’s The Diving Bell and the Butterfly, Kamiński took another phenomenal visual approach to depict the story of a man with locked-in syndrome, only able to see the world through a single functioning eye. In the film, won Camerimage’s Golden Frog honor in 2007, the lens shifts sharply in and out of focus, blurring most of the field of vision while some details pop with intense clarity.

“The script, and the book it was based on, are great,” says Kamiński, but provided little guidance. “The whole description is: ‘The hero returns from darkness, from being unconscious for the last two weeks, and starts seeing the world through one eye.’ That’s it.”

Despite certain aesthetic preferences — ”I do like strong light, particularly backlight, I like characters in half-light, going into and out of the shadows. I like smoke” he says — Kamiński does not have a signature look. His approach is film follows function. Cold blues and metallic shadows to evoke the tech-dystopia of Minority Report. Retro pastels and smooth tracking shots to make the 60s swing in Catch Me If You Can. Grainy, handheld shots of muted oranges and browns in Munich to give the story the feel of a 1970s conspiracy thriller.

The Kamiński/Spielberg collaboration, which now stretches over 30 years and more than 20 films, has to count as one of the most significant artistic collaborations in American cinema history. His work with Kamiński marks the second phase of Spielberg’s career, as the director moved from glossy, classical Hollywood imagery, sharp lights and bright colors, to a grittier, more naturalistic style, appropriate to the more mature, morally-ambivalent stories he wanted to tell.

Kamiński does not claim credit for the director’s evolution. “Steven was not ready to do Schindler’s List until he was ready,” he says. “He was moving that way and I entered his life at the right point where he was able to accept the aesthetics I gave him and embrace them. I think what he saw in me was someone new with a new point of view, someone who wasn’t biased by Hollywood, with a fresh approach. He saw me as a partner. And I saw him as a partner.”

The partnership continues on Spielberg’s latest, Disclosure Day, which has Kamiński working in a different register. “As I’m getting older, things are becoming more simplistic,” he says. “I want to go slightly more reserved, relaxed.”

For the film, a sci-fi thriller about aliens, but set in the present day, he says he aimed for “something more naturalistic, more contemporary.” In one scene, in a safe house, a gray, very direct light comes through the window, slightly green, with a little flare in the background. “It’s got austerity in the images,” Kamiński says, “and that comes from growing up in Poland, with the images from my childhood.”

Next up is another collaboration with Spielberg, on an untitled Western, the director’s first, which Spielberg hopes to shoot next year. Kamiński is already imagining the landscape, drawing, as always, from the world he grew up in.

“We used to go to this region in the Sudeten Mountains, where it was just beautiful, rolling hills, looked like parts of Montana,” he says. “The lay of the land, the snow on the ground, the fog.” All these elements exist in America too, he acknowledges, but “those who shoot American movies tend to come from somewhere else, and we see these same things differently. That’s why there’s room in this profession for men and women from different countries who bring different aesthetics to American movies.”

#713. China lays out plans to land astronauts on the moon 'before 2030.' Can NASA still win this race?

The Chinese roadmap includes an uncrewed lunar landing in 2028.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

China has given us some details about the epic moon landing it plans to pull off a few years from now.

Chinese officials laid out the roadmap for its crewed lunar campaign at the 7th Manned Space Symposium, which was held Oct. 31 and Nov. 1 in Beijing. The campaign consists of four missions, culminating in a crewed touchdown "before 2030," according to media reports.

That timeline — which is consistent with previous statements made by the China Manned Space Agency — keeps the pressure on the U.S., which aims to put its own astronauts down on the moon in 2028, via NASA's Artemis program.

Leaked slide confirms the four-mission progression toward China’s crewed lunar landing: 🚀2027: Maiden flight of Long March 10A carrying Mengzhou CSS cargo resupply mission, to validate the new human-rated vehicle and Mengzhou’s orbital operations in LEO. 🚀2028: First flight of the heavier CZ-10 with an uncrewed Lanyue lander performing a lunar descent and ascent test, exercising the lander’s propulsion and guidance. 🚀🚀2029: Dual CZ-10 launches of Mengzhou and Lanyue for a full-scale lunar-orbit rehearsal, demonstrating rendezvous, docking, and integrated operations. 🚀🚀Before the end of 2030: Dual CZ-10 crewed lunar landing mission.November 1, 2026

The first mission in China's four-part lunar campaign is scheduled to fly in 2027, according to CNSpaceflight, an X account that keeps a close eye on China's activities in space. The outlet cited an X user who shared a presentation slide of the plan.

That launch — the first of of China's new Long March 10A rocket — will send an uncrewed Mengzhou spacecraft to low Earth orbit (LEO) for a series of tests. Mengzhou, whose name means "Dream Vessel," is the next-gen crew capsule that will carry Chinese astronauts to lunar orbit.

Mission number two, launching in 2028, will involve a different set of hardware — the more powerful Long March 10 rocket and the Lanyue ("Embracing the Moon") lunar lander. This will also be an uncrewed flight, and it will mark the debut of the Long March 10, which will send Lanyue to orbit around the moon. If all goes to plan, Lanyue will touch down on the moon and then launch itself back to lunar orbit.

Mission number three, flying in 2029, will also target an uncrewed lunar landing, but it will feature two Long March 10 launches — one apiece for Mengzhou and Lanyue. The two spacecraft will conduct a rendezvous and docking rehearsal in lunar orbit, then separate for Lanyue's trip down to the surface.

This will set the stage for mission four — the real deal, in which two Long March 10s launch a crewed Mengzhou and an uncrewed Lanyue "before 2030." The two vessels will dock in lunar orbit, and the astronauts will move into Lanyue for their historic lunar landing.

Three astronauts will apparently launch on Mengzhou, and two of them will land on the moon aboard Lanyue, according to CNSpaceflight. The duo will spend three days on the lunar surface, conducting moonwalks on each of those days.

And about that "before 2030" timeline: The wording may have been chosen very carefully.

"One reading is that 2029 coincides with the 80th anniversary of the current government, creating a strong internal incentive to achieve the landing that year. At the same time, the technical schedule (new Long March 10 family, Mengzhou, Lanyue, dual-launch operations) remains aggressive; committing publicly to 2029 would create significant political exposure if any major test slips," CNSpaceflight wrote in a Nov. 2 X post.

"Using 'before 2030' therefore functions as deliberate wording flexibility: a 2029 landing can still be presented as an early historic success, while a slip into 2030 remains inside the stated goal without requiring a formal target revision. You just need to put 'year-end' after 'before 2030,'" the outlet added.

NASA's Artemis program has already sent astronauts around the moon, doing so this past April on the Artemis II mission. The agency is currently gearing up for Artemis III, a crewed flight to LEO that will test rendezvous and docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's two private crewed landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

Artemis III is currently on track to fly in the summer of 2027, NASA officials have said. But an on-time liftoff is far from guaranteed, as both Starship and Blue Moon still have some boxes to check.

Starship just reached Earth orbit for the first time on Sept. 28, for example, and it has yet to demonstrate off-Earth refueling, which will be a crucial part of any Starship mission beyond Earth orbit. And Blue Moon has yet to leave the ground at all. The Blue Origin lander is scheduled to fly for the first time next spring, on an uncrewed test mission that will send it to the lunar surface.

If all goes well on Artemis III, NASA will be clear to start prepping for Artemis IV, which will put astronauts down near the lunar south pole aboard either Starship or Blue Moon. (It's unclear at the moment which lander NASA will choose.)

NASA is currently targeting early 2028 for the launch of Artemis IV. If that schedule holds, the agency will beat China and pull off the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 back in 1972.

But the new moon race won't end there, because this one isn't all about flags and footprints. Both NASA and China aim to build bases on the lunar surface over the next decade or so, setting up humanity's first true outpost on a world beyond Earth. The stakes are high, NASA and U.S. military officials have stressed: Whoever does so first can claim the best spots and get the best access to key lunar resources such as water ice. The leader will also get to establish norms of behavior on the moon, which at the moment is a bit of a Wild West of exploration.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. #712. Bayern Munich's Kenya friendly highlights Africa's growing pull for global sport

Bayern Munich are to open Nairobi's new Raila Odinga International Stadium against Ajax as Kenya prepares for AFCON 2027. The match highlights Africa's growing sports ambitions — and questions over cost and legacy.

Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich are to travel to Nairobi, Kenya during the winter break to play a friendly that opens the newly finished Raila Odinga International Stadium in the capital city. The German side will face Ajax Amsterdam as the game acts as part of the country's preparations for the 2027 African Cup of Nations (AFCON), which will be held in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania next summer.

"Bayern has millions of fantastic fans in Africa with whom we feel a close connection – it's a continent with a huge passion for football," Rouven Kasper, Bayern board member for marketing and sales, said in a club statement.

"We will be making a further contribution to raising the profile of the Bundesliga and are very much looking forward to this special event."

The news is just the latest venture into global sports investing in Africa. Earlier this month, Formula 1 announced it was returning to the continent after Rwanda secured the rights for a deal from the early 2030s onwards. In September, World Athletics revealed Nairobi would host the World Championships in 2029. It will be the first time the event has been held in Africa.

Simon Chadwick, a business management and program director at the African School of Economics, believes that over the last two decades the professionalization and industrialization of sports has begun to emerge in Africa.

"Countries like Rwanda, Kenya, Morocco and obviously, South Africa, if we go back to the last decade of the previous century, have increasingly begun to deploy sport as a policy instrument," Chadwick told DW, adding Senegal and Egypt to the list.

"There are these image and reputational benefits which very often are bundled up as soft power. It's about attractiveness and appeal and engagement," said Chadwick.

"It's almost like a kind of professionalization, industrialization and politicization of sport that we're seeing elsewhere in the world has now arrived in Africa. We are seeing a much greater sense of kind of self-determination within Africa to do this," he added.

"This is not just about sport. It is also about diplomacy and bilateral trade, but also about the broader economic and industrial context within which sport sits."

For Kenya specifically, the building of the stadium is in line with the housing and sports infrastructural development that has been so heavily promoted under President William Ruto. Hosting this game is a symbol of the development currently happening in Nairobi.

"The bigger picture is that Nairobi now is positioning itself as a as an alternative sports venue," Richard Wanjohi, Editorial and Research Lead at the African Sports and Creative Institute (ASCI), told DW.

"I think we have seen what Kigali has done over the last number of years. For us to then come back into this conversation as a major city that can host such an event, it's huge. A few weeks later, we'll have the rugby sevens series again and then ultimately, the Africa Cup of Nations in July."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chadwick believes that unlike Rwanda, Kenya's relative stability and pre-existing tourist industry allows for a more natural development of sports investment.

"This is not Kenya trying to build a tourism industry through an engagement in sport. I think it's an extension of what Kenya has been doing for a number of years through sport."

Combined with being a multi-sport country - athletics, rugby, football, volleyball – Wanjohi believes Kenya is ready to make the most of that performance on the field or track.

"It's about time that we also host the world and show them that we can do this from a hosting perspective, but also from developing infrastructure that is ready to host such sports events," Wanjohi said.

"It's beyond just saying that we have the talent that is already in the sport, but it's saying that we have the infrastructure, we have the skills, we have the capability to host this as any other African, if not global nation."

However, Ruto's government has been criticized over taxation, unemployment and its handling of dissent. Given that this stadium cost approximately €375 million ($418 million), it is perhaps no surprise that questions are being asked about the decision to invest in major sports infrastructure.

"People are asking, we are a struggling economy. There are a lot of other issues that could be addressed, like the education sector, health and all that. How did we get that money and be able to make that provision? Also interestingly, is that there's an appearance fee that is going to be paid to both Bayern and Ajax," said Wanjohi, who added there was also some frustration that the opening game was not given to local teams or even the national side.

Ultimately, the timing of this also matters. While many sports fans in the country are excited, others are critical.

"The government knows that this is almost like a campaign tool. We have an election coming up in August next year so the government or the president of the day obviously wants to use as much leverage of such an event to milk it for all it's worth," Wanjohi added.

"So the two different schools of thought are: It's a good thing to have, but at what cost are we doing it at and is it in the public interest as well?"

The proof will be in what the legacy of events like Bayern Munich's friendly in Nairobi brings Kenyan football. The feeling in late 2026 though, is largely optimistic.

"I guess the acid test is that many African nations carry with them the baggage from the past that this is just trophy asset investment that is ultimately going to create white, white elephant infrastructure," Chadwick said.

"But having spoken to people in Kenyan sport, in the industry itself, it seems to me that there is a genuine appetite for sports to become a genuine and legitimate driver of economic activity."

Janek Speight contributed reporting for this article.

#711. Judi Dench Says Vin Diesel Sent Her Flowers ‘the Length of a Kayak’ to Persuade Her to Join ‘The Chronicles of Riddick’: I’m ‘Far Too Easily Wooed’

Judi Dench can’t say no to a big bouquet of flowers, especially if they’re kayak-sized and come from Vin Diesel.

“He came to see me at the Haymarket Theatre to ask if I’d be in ‘The Chronicles of Riddick,’” Dench wrote in her new memoir, “Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?” “Before he arrived, he sent me such a massive bunch of flowers. They couldn’t get them up the stairs to my dressing room, so they had to leave them at the stage door. They were easily the length of a kayak. And as wide.” Related Stories Paramount Network Orders 13 Original Episodes of Larry the Cable Guy-Hosted Clip Show 'American Mayhem' (EXCLUSIVE)

“You can’t say no to a man like that, can you?” she joked, adding, “I’m cheap as chips, me. Far too easily wooed.”

Convinced by the gesture, Dench went on to play Aereon in the 2004 film, the elemental ambassador who guides Riddick (Diesel) through his tumultuous travels to rescue his old allies and confront the head of the Necromonger empire.

This wasn’t the first time gifts wooed the 91-year-old actress into a role. She also revealed Kenneth Branagh gave her “the most wonderful embroidered handkerchief when he asked me to be in ‘[Murder on the] Orient Express’ — with the character’s initials on it.”

“He must’ve known that’d make me say yes; he’s so sneaky. But then I’d do anything for Ken. If he said, ‘Will you play a mat on the floor in Three Sisters?’ I’d say, ‘When do I start?’” she said. “Then, of course, little by little, I found out who else was involved in ‘Orient Express’: Olivia Colman, Penélope Cruz, Johnny Depp, Derek Jacobi … How could I resist?”

Dench played Princess Natalia Dragomiroff in the 2017 mystery-drama but said she had mixed feelings about the character.

“Don’t ask me anything about her. She was some old broad who sat around with a lot of jewelry and a couple of Shih Tzus — one black, one white,” Dench said.

#710. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Powers $31M in Historic Box Office Launch Against Subdued ‘Cat in the Hat’

The sequel to 2023's 'Godzilla Minus One' made noise as 'Ramayana' and 'Wild Horse Nine' also debuted.

Godzilla Minus Zero is king of the box office in its opening weekend as the sequel feature tallies the biggest launch in its distributor’s history with nearly three times the debut of predecessor Godzilla Minus One. Meanwhile, The Cat in the Hat got off to a quieter start.

Hitting 3,254 North American theaters from GKids and Toho, Godzilla Minus Zero conquered $31.6 million domestically for the weekend. This is being touted as the highest-grossing live-action foreign-language opening at the box office since 2004’s Hero launched with $17.8 million. (It’s behind the debut of last year’s animated Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle with $70.6 million, while 2004’s The Passion of the Christ and its massive $83.8 million opening is not included in the category as an American-produced project.) Godzilla Minus Zero notches the highest-grossing opening weekend for a GKids release, topping the $13 million for 2023’s Oscar-winning The Boy and the Heron. Related Stories TV Druski Embodies Elizabeth Holmes in 'You Can See Everything' Spoof on 'SNL' Movies Danny McBride's 'G.I. Joe' Movie Lands 2028 Release From Paramount

As the first-ever Japanese production filmed for Imax, Godzilla Minus Zero collected $12 million domestically from the premium format, comprising an eye-popping 40 percent of the domestic haul. It added $31.4 million internationally, including $17 million in Japan. Filmmaker Takashi Yamazaki‘s sequel to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One earned an A CinemaScore from audiences and performed well above the distributor’s projected domestic opening in the mid-$20 millions.

“This landmark release is the result of a thoughtful campaign by GKids and Toho that emphasized the ‘must see’ intensity of the theatrical experience and director Takashi Yamazaki’s vision,” GKids vp of distribution Chance Huskey said in a statement. “We’re so happy to see audiences embrace Godzilla Minus Zero at an unprecedented scale for an international film.”

Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe and Min Tanaka star in the new movie that carries a reported budget in the mid-teens. It centers on postwar Japan dealing with attacks from the three-headed Ghidorah and the possibility of Godzilla’s return. Godzilla Minus Zero holds an impressive 90 percent critics approval on Rotten Tomatoes, along with a 96 from audiences, with The Hollywood Reporter chief film critic David Rooney calling it a “thrilling jolt of marauding monster action.”

The sequel is making a bigger footprint than Godzilla Minus One, which opened in December 2023 with $11.4 million domestically and reached $57.1 million for the run, adding $56.9 million internationally. The film rode its massive breakout success to become Japan’s first feature to win the best visual effects Oscar.

“A huge thank you to everyone who ran to the theaters the moment the film opened!” added Yamazaki about the sequel. “I grew up in awe of Hollywood movies and have spent my career chasing after them, so seeing our Godzilla welcomed with so much warmth and excitement by people all over the world, and watched by so many of you, honestly feels like a dream.”

Overall, the weekend’s titles collected a combined $121.7 million, showing an increase of around 98 percent over last weekend, with the studios avoiding new releases for the Halloween frame, and a roughly 45 percent uptick from the equivalent 2025 weekend that saw the debut of 20 Century’s Predator: Badlands, according to Rentrak. The 2026 domestic total stands at $8.625 billion, which is 20.6 percent above last year’s same stretch, despite this October having had trouble establishing hits that can continue to play deep into the fall.

Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat grossed a sleepy $20.5 million domestically from 4,003 North American locations, on par with the studio’s projection. The two previous animated Dr. Seuss adaptations had far higher debuts, with Universal’s 2018 The Grinch swiping $67.5 million in its opening, while that studio’s 2012 launch of The Lorax claimed $70.2 million. The studio hopes for word of mouth to help the $92 million-budgeted The Cat in the Hat play through the Thanksgiving holiday and into December after earning an A CinemaScore, with competition on the horizon from Disney’s Hexed on Nov. 25.

The Cat in the Hat could join the list of Warner Bros.’ 2026 theatrical disappointments, following such releases as The Bride! and Digger, unless it shows impressive legs. Dr. Seuss films historically haven’t made a big splash overseas, and this one has staggered its international release, with around half of the territories set for later debuts throughout the remainder of the year. The Cat in the Hat added $10 million internationally for the frame.

Directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni’s animated adaptation of Dr. Seuss’ classic 1957 children’s book centers on the titular feline being given a final chance to prove his worth by helping a pair of siblings. Bill Hader leads the voice cast that also includes Matt Berry, Quinta Brunson and Xochitl Gomez. The movie marks Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s first title since Bill Damaschke took over as president and chief creative officer in 2023.

Critics have been a bit aloof on the film, as it holds a 46 percent Rotten Tomatoes score from reviewers and an 87 percent score from audiences, with THR critic Frank Scheck calling it “more taxing than enjoyable.” It’s faring better critically than Universal’s 2003 live-action The Cat in the Hat starring Mike Myers, which holds an 11 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes. That movie opened to $38.3 million domestically en route to a North American cume of $101 million against a $109 million budget.

Sony Pictures released Prime Focus Studios’ Ramayana: Rise of a Legend in 1,433 North American locations, with the film grossing roughly $8.6 million for the weekend and $12.1 million for the four days. It added $32 million in India and an additional $11.5 million from 37 overseas markets. Boasting the widest domestic launch ever for an Indian movie, director Nitesh Tiwari’s religious epic focuses on the life of Prince Rama, with the two-film project’s budget reported at $420 million and beyond. It holds a 76 score from critics on Rotten Tomatoes, along with an 89 from audiences.

Also debuting in the top five is Angel Studios’ Drummer Boy, with directors Ben and Joel David Smallbone’s historical drama grossing a strong $9.3 million from 2,850 North American locations. Earning an A CinemaScore, the faith-based musical focuses on an unlikely bond during the American Revolution and stars Joel David Smallbone in the title role. On Rotten Tomatoes, it has a 50 critics score and a 94 from audiences. Angel was uniquely positioned to open the film in a major way after having established itself with the faith-minded audience.

“It has been eight long years of failure and triumph to bring Drummer Boy to the screen,” Joel David Smallbone said in a statement to celebrate the opening. “So as you’d imagine, I find myself deeply impacted by the fact that this personal story has found its way into hundreds of thousands of your hearts.”

Academy Awards hopeful Wild Horse Nine opened in 1,100 North American theaters with an estimated frame of $6 million. John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell and Steve Buscemi lead writer-director Martin McDonagh’s comedic thriller about two CIA operatives who travel from Santiago, Chile, to Easter Island in 1973. The Searchlight Pictures release holds a 94 critics score on Rotten Tomatoes and 91 from audiences, with Rooney’s review describing it as “uniquely affecting.”

Expected to hit just outside the top 10 is Burns & Co and Fathom Entertainment’s Jimmy, with the Jimmy Stewart biopic opening to an estimated $2 million from 1,470 North American theaters. Scheck’s review calls star KJ Apa “top-notch” but deems director Aaron Burns’ film “heartfelt to a fault.”

Another Oscar hopeful launched in platform release as A24 debuted Club Kid on six screens, with the Cannes standout grossing $390,583 for an average of $65,097 per screen that topped the weekend. Making his feature directorial debut, Jordan Firstman also stars as a party promoter who learns he has a 10-year-old son. Set to expand into Thanksgiving, it boasts a sterling 100 score from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes, with THR critic Richard Lawson heralding it as “winning and clever.”

Amazon MGM Studios releases I Play Rocky in seven locations, and it grossed around $345,000 for a per-screen average of $49,200. Anthony Ippolito stars as Sylvester Stallone in director Peter Farrelly’s making-of story for the 1976 classic Rocky. In his review, Rooney wrote that the movie — which holds an 88 Rotten Tomatoes score from critics — creates “a wave of warm nostalgia.”

Among holdovers, A24’s much-discussed Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything looks to pull in around $8.8 million for the weekend as it jostles with Ramayana and Drummer Boy to round out the top five. The domestic cume for directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s feature stands at $79.7 million.

Likely rounding out the top 10 is Black Bear’s Wicker, which declined just 23 percent in its third weekend with $3.3 million for a domestic cume of $19.8 million, along with an additional $9.1 million internationally. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard lead directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s romantic fantasy that continues to build on enthusiastic word of mouth, holding a 94 critics score on Rotten Tomatoes and 92 from audiences.

Next weekend brings the Johnny Depp studio comeback vehicle Ebenezer, along with How to Rob a Bank and Paper Tiger.

This story was first published on Nov. 7 at 8:43 a.m.

#709. Sanfic Prizes: ‘Monguen’ and ‘Narciso’ Win at Pared-Back Ceremony Due to Sudden Demise of ‘A Fantastic Woman’ Director Sebastian Lelio

The unexpected demise Nov. 6 of Chile’s Oscar-winning Sebastián Lelio (“A Fantastic Woman”) cast a pall over the closing ceremonies of both the festival and industry section of the Santiago Film Festival (Sanfic), which wraps Nov. 8.

The red carpet portions of the industry and festival ceremonies held Nov. 6 and 7, respectively, were cancelled. “We dedicate the rest of this festival to Sebastián,” said festival director Carlos Nuñez and Sanfic Industria head Gabriela Sandoval, both visibly bereft. “His films will remain as his legacy but his passing is incredibly painful, especially because he had been so close to the festival since its very beginning,” said Nuñez. Related Stories Paramount Network Orders 13 Original Episodes of Larry the Cable Guy-Hosted Clip Show 'American Mayhem' (EXCLUSIVE)

Lelio’s family announced that the Cineteca Nacional (National Film Library) would be open to all those who wished to pay their respects this weekend. Real life also reminded some festival goers of Lelio’s last film, musical “The Wave” (“La ola”), which dealt with Chile’s violent 2018 student protests, when tear gas met some panel participants as they stepped out of a university. The students were protesting the latest move by the right-wing government of President Kast, whose system-wide budget cuts include education. They also called for the resignation of Justice Minister Fernando Rabat to resign over his sentence reductions for child sex offenders and human rights violators.

Among the nine Chilean pics in competition, the Best Picture award went to documentary “Monguen” by the late Antonio Caro who also died suddenly while working on his film, which led his producer to take over. Lelio was filming an adaptation of Alejandro Zambra’s novel “Chilean Poet” for Fabula and was also in pre-production on “Voyagers,” featuring Andrew Garfield and Daisy Edgar-Jones.

“I think this is a well-deserved recognition for ‘Monguen,’ a film that explores stories from the margins. It deals with a subject rarely addressed in Chilean cinema: Mapuche culture, the culture of the south and characters who don’t often get represented on screen. In this film, Antonio Caro brings those worlds to life and allows us to gain a deeper understanding of the culture of southern Chile,” Nuñez told Variety.

Best Chilean Director honors went to Thomas Woodroffe for his debut feature “Erratics” (“Bloques erráticos”), a subtle film that features French actor Denis Lavant. Lavant playing filmmaker Lucien Castelnau’s ghost who has been released from a glacier after a century into a futuristic Patagonia where technological advances collide with overlooked histories.

“He’s definitely a director to watch, and someone whose approach to cinema we find very compelling,” said Nuñez.

A tearful Paulina Garcia, accepting the Best Actress award for her role in “Love is the Monster” paid tribute to Lelio, displaying the Berlin Silver Bear statuette that she won for her performance in his 2013 drama, “Gloria.”

Among the international pics in competition, Paraguayan Marcelo Martinessi’s historical drama “Narciso” won Best Feature. Based on the eponymous novel by Guido Rodríguez Alcalá, it relates the story of a Paraguayan LGBT rock star who is found dead at the peak of his career. Through the prism of music and art, the drama explores facets of Asunción society during the dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner.

“Martinessi is one of the most interesting filmmakers to emerge from Paraguay in recent years,” said Nuñez, adding: “We felt it was an important Latin American film to include, particularly given how little cinema is produced in Paraguay. Martinessi is one of the country’s most compelling voices, so the award felt thoroughly deserved.”

The Best Short recognition. from the 21 shorts in contention, went to Ariel Amor’s “Reina de Puerto,” set in Valparaiso where a 60-year-old trans woman forms a bond with young drifter.

The good news for the festival was that it saw a 10%-15% uptick in attendance, with final figures hovering between 35,000 to 40,000. “It’s been a very lively week, with filmmakers, cast members, actors and actresses introducing their films and meeting audiences. There’s been a real buzz around the festival, and we’ve seen packed cinemas,” said Nuñez.

Meanwhile, Sanfic Industria unveiled a slew of awards, mostly in kind, to its over 100 participants in a variety of sections.

Honors at the genre project competition were split pretty evenly between three titles: folk horror/urban realism mix “Tonalli,” set in Mexico City’s hard-scrabble district of Tepito; the sadistic “The Hostess,” the return of extreme horror helmer Roberto San Sebastian and “L4IK4,” a 2D, stop motion and pixilation virtual world odyssey set in an alternate Cold War universe which marks the feature debut of rising Chilean animation star Simon Bucher. Most notably perhaps, “Tonalli” scored a co-production prize from co-organizer Mórbido.

At WIP Iberoamericana, Sanfic Industria’s industry centerpiece, bearing out buzz “Hot Springs,” the feature debut of DP-turned-helmer Armin Marchesini Weihmuller, took swept three prizes, including the only cash prize on offer.

Produced by Argentina’s Gema Films, the film weighs in as a touching hybrid portrait of Evangelina and brother Luis, both over 80, vacationing briefly at a hot springs hotel spa – an affecting vision of old age, its infirmities, bedrock relationships and a resilient zest for life.

The sophomore outing of Yull Núñez, Indigenous eco-thriller “The Cry of Serankwa,” where a mining project in Colombia’s highest mountains confronts two former best friends, also scored a trio of awards.

WIP Iberoamericana also served recognition to Fernando Lavanderos’ “The Grass Along the Path,” an engaging but bittersweet teen love story set in 1990 which, thanks to the repeated on screen interruptions of the film’s crew, works as meta reflection of how Chile and film viewing have changed in the last 36 years.

Kudos spread wide with an Egeda cash prize going to Nicolas Acuña’s “Skin,” a custody battle three-way co-production from ‘Besieged’ producer Promocine.

Rita Hostt’s debut feature, a summer romance fantasy, took home the Syncro Fiction award towards its musical supervisión. The 1930-set historical drama “The Girl” (“La Niña”) from Sergio Castro San Martín and cancer survival documentary “La fragilidad de los cangrejos” won two awards each.

Alex de la Iglesia Talks About First Shoot in Chile

Spain’s Alex de la Iglesia visited the festival to talk about his absurdist comedy “The Misunderstanding” (“El Malentendido”) pointing out that it was his first time to shoot in Chile and thanked the festival for bringing him over last year for a Masterclass where he met his Chilean producer, Pablo Díaz of Rio Estudios (“Hidden Island”). “Sanfic set everything in motion and made all of this possible,” he said. The farce, which blends the Marx Brothers’ sardonic humor with the existential anguish of a war film, will be shooting in Santiago and its environs for the next four weeks, starting Nov. 9. “The Misundertanding” stars Benjamin Vicuña, who Iglesia worked with on his upcoming Netflix pic “Felicidades” in Buenos Aires.

Grupo Mórbido’s Pablo Guisa, Sitges’ Monica Garcia and Docs Mx’s Arizbeth Becerril Discuss Bringing Projects to a Global Audience

Among the most popular panels in the festival, its overriding theme was the need to bridge artistic ambition and commercial realities. Grupo Mórbido’s Pablo Guisa stressed that industry platforms must focus on getting films made, not simply moving projects from one lab to another. He said: “I’m not interested in being a cultural travel agent.” He argued that projects need both artistic value and commercial potential to lure financing.

The panelists also questioned the growing influence of streaming platforms and algorithms, whose decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Guisa encouraged filmmakers to trust their creative instincts rather than chase trends, while Arizbeth Becerril of DocsMX reminded the audience: “We don’t have a fucking clue” what the algorithm wants.

Despite the evolving changes in viewing habits, festivals remain essential spaces for discovery, networking and collective experiences, they pointed out. Sitges Film Fest director general Mónica García underscored their ability to offer something streaming cannot replicate: “Visibility and legitimacy,” stressing the importance of the theatrical experience and the sense of community they create.

Among the first pickups at Sanfic Industria, Latin American distributor Cineplex boarded two projects at Sanfic’s pix-in-post section, WIP Iberoamericana: Panama-set “La Residencia,” written, directed and produced by Mariel García Spooner (“Algo azul”), and Indigenous eco-thriller “The Cry of Serankwa” by Yull Nuñez, whose three awards in kind will help him complete his lauded project.

Cineplex picked up both North and South American sales rights to “La Residencia,” which Cineplex managing partner Diana Dudek said “has the potential to resonate with international audiences.” “We immediately connected with the story of these three friends who, at a more mature stage of their lives, decide to reinvent themselves and move forward together.”

For “The Cry of Serankwa,” to which Cineplex acquired Colombian and Latin American rights, they said: “We felt a strong connection to its story and its portrayal of the sacred territories of Colombia’s Iku, Wiwa and Kogui communities in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.”

NASA has revealed a glimpse of its next X-plane, known as the X-70 Fractal.

Or at least what it thinks the X-70 will look like once built. The agency released a short statement on Wednesday (Nov. 4) announcing the X-plane, or experimental plane, declaring it to be a highly maneuverable test bed with a "rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology," allowing NASA to swap both external and internal components on-the-fly. This modular architecture will allow NASA to "explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight," according to the agency's statement.

The announcement was made alongside an AI-generated image showing two canted vertical tail fins emerging from swirling smoke. Little can be gleaned from the image about what final form the X-70 might take, but the tail fins are somewhat reminiscent of the Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor or Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet.

"The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in the statement. The NASA chief called the aircraft "just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics" and said that the agency expects the X-70 to make its first flight within two years.

"This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly," Isaacman added.

NASA's statement fleshes out a few details about the X-70's capabilities. According to the agency, Fractal will fly at a cruise speed of Mach .75, about the same as a Boeing 737 Classic. The X-70 will be able to reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet (13.7 kilometers), and will have a range exceeding 1,726 miles (2,777 kilometers, or 1,500 nautical miles).

The X-70 Fractal will also be able to carry around 2,000 pounds (900 kg) of experimental payloads both internally and externally, which will allow for a "wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities," NASA said in the statement.

NASA adds it will have a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds (4,535 kilograms), around the same weight as the Scaled Composites- and Northrop Grumman-developed Model 437 Vanguard experimental aircraft. In fact, the two aircraft share a similar silhouette — at least in the AI image of the X-70 Fractal NASA has released so far.

The agency's most recent X-plane, the X-59, has been flying for over a year. That jet features a radical long-nosed geometry without a forward windscreen; pilots fly by way of an augmented reality screen that combines views from sensors and a forward-facing camera.

That geometry dampens the shockwaves coming off of the X-59 when it flies faster than the sound barrier, allowing it to fly at speeds over Mach 1 without the thunderous sonic booms that typically accompany supersonic flight.

There are numerous experimental aircraft being developed by private companies, such as Boom Supersonic's X-1 jet, which, like the X-59, aims to develop technologies that lessen the auditory impact of sonic booms on the ground.

In terms of other government X-plane projects, Boeing is working on the F-47, a next-generation stealth fighter for use by the U.S. military, and DARPA, the Pentagon's research agency, has an X-plane project of its own known as CRANE.

Brett is curious about emerging aerospace technologies, alternative launch concepts, military space developments and uncrewed aircraft systems. Brett's work has appeared on Scientific American, The War Zone, Popular Science, the History Channel, Science Discovery and more. Brett has degrees from Clemson University and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. In his free time, Brett enjoys skywatching throughout the dark skies of the Appalachian mountains.

#707. THR Visionary: 5 Janusz Kaminski Shots

The cinematographer, this year’s THR Visionary Award honoree, always lets film follow function, choosing a visual style to match the story being told.

Try to find a signature Janusz Kaminski “look” and you’ll come up empty. Yes, he likes backlighting and has a penchant for smoke and film-noir style. But the Polish-born cameraman, winner of the 2026 THR Visionary Award for excellence in cinematography, has spent three decades making images that bend to the story rather than the other way around.

Kaminski’s guiding principle is that form follows function. With lenses, film stocks, color palettes and camera movement chosen to serve what each film needs to tell its story. The result is a body of work remarkable for its originality and visual diversity. Here are five of Kaminski’s most original visions. Related Stories Movies Janusz Kaminski, the Polish Cameraman Who Taught Hollywood How to See Movies To Make a Doc About a Nomadic Cyclist, the 'Perfect Road' Filmmakers Spent 3 Months in a Campervan

Steven Spielberg’s Holocaust drama was shot in stark black-and-white. The choice wasn’t nostalgic but a way of conjuring newsreels and documentary record, with a handheld immediacy that keeps the audience in the room with the horror. Kaminski’s hard, contrasty lighting, harsh shadows and drifting smoke owe a debt to German Expressionism and postwar European cinema. Against this monochrome, the lone splash of color, the little girl’s red coat, lands as one of the most devastating images in modern film. It won him his first Oscar.

For the Omaha Beach landing and the war that follows, Kaminski set out to make combat look like frontline footage rather than a Hollywood spectacle. Colors are leached out to a washed, metallic palette. He stripped protective coatings from his lenses to invite flare and a rawer, less polished image, and used a narrow shutter angle that makes explosions and bullet strikes snap with a jittery, staccato clarity. Handheld cameras and spattered lenses put the viewer on the sand with the soldiers. The look was so influential that it reshaped how war was filmed for a generation, and it earned him a second Oscar.

In Julian Schnabel’s adaptation of Jean-Dominique Bauby’s memoir, written by a man paralyzed but for one eyelid, the camera becomes that eye. Kaminski opens the film from Bauby’s first-person perspective: blurred focus, tilted frames, sudden blinks and a claustrophobic narrowness of vision that gradually widens. As Bauby’s imagination takes flight, so does the imagery. Soft, luminous pastels and sunlit memories of Paris and the seaside offer escape from the hospital room. It’s an exercise in subjective cinematography that earned Kaminski an Oscar nomination.

If Saving Private Ryan rejected glossy spectacle, War Horse embraced it on purpose. Spielberg and Kaminski drew on the sweeping, painterly look of classic Hollywood Westerns and epics, with John Ford and David Lean in mind. Anamorphic widescreen frames showcase burnished golds, glowing skies and silhouetted figures against vast landscapes, giving the First World War tale a storybook romanticism before the mud and horror close in. It’s lush, deliberately old-fashioned and entirely suited to a story told through the eyes of a horse. It was another Oscar-nominated turn.

For Spielberg’s tense thriller about the aftermath of the 1972 Olympics massacre, Kaminski looked to the gritty, paranoid cinema of the 1970s. The film has a grainy, slightly faded texture with muted, earthy colors, and frequently uses zoom lenses, a hallmark of the era’s thrillers, to create a sense of surveillance and unease. The images feel period-authentic without becoming pastiche, and their rough-edged restraint keeps the focus on the moral toll of the mission.
